guard: A hosted runtime create or status request is decided only for a manager actor whose own ledger row holds supervise, at its own instance's current open manager gate, at the current serve epoch, with the host-issued registration proof, for a target owned by the authenticated owner; both closed schemas refuse any provider reference; the decision carries only owner, instanceId, actor and target; stock refuses both kinds rather than answering them
why: The ledger mutation decides without reading the manager actor's ledger row. A host composing the door would then authorize a manager actor the owner never granted; the suite names the cell for an actor with no row.
The supervise mutation accepts any row. spawn and admin are ordinary agent capabilities, and the suite proves a row holding both is still refused.

The current-registration mutation skips the gate, principal, epoch, and proof check at the runtime door. managed-agent-enrollment.json grades that shared check one guard at a time; this mutation proves the runtime door reaches it, since without it a create could launch a runtime for a frozen, foreign, or superseded registration on a forged proof.
The target-owner mutation lets a request name another owner's target, which would let one owner's manager drive or read another owner's runtime.

The two closed-schema mutations let a providerRef through at the top level or a handle through in the target. The contract refuses a provider reference rather than ignoring it, so a host can never be handed one as if it were authority.
The dispatch mutation removes the unimplemented refusal, so a runtime request falls through to the manager-lifecycle issuer.

The target-serialization mutation restores the JSON.stringify comparison of the result target. Property order is not part of the closed target schema, so a host that serializes the same owner, actor and lifecycleUid in another order would have its answer refused as a foreign target.
